Wasp\'s built-in background job executor, **PgBoss**, only works on PostgreSQL, so once the migration is done you must also add a PgBoss background job to justify (and exercise) the new database.  The project is a classic Wasp project: a `main.wasp` declaration file, a separate `schema.prisma` file that holds the datasource/models, a `migrations/` directory with the current SQLite migrations, and the React/Node source under `src/`. The app has a `Task` entity, a `getTasks` query, a `createTask` action, a page that lists and adds tasks, and a custom HTTP API endpoint `GET /api/stats`.  ## Requirements - Switch the app\'s database from SQLite to PostgreSQL. - Point the app at the **local** PostgreSQL server that is already running in this environment. - Regenerate the database migrations so they are PostgreSQL migrations (the old SQLite migrations cannot be reused). - Keep the existing functionality working after the migration: the task list (query + action) and the `GET /api/stats` endpoint must still work. - Add a background **job** that uses the **PgBoss** executor and runs automatically, exactly once, every time the server starts. This is only possible because the app now runs on PostgreSQL. - The app must still build and run with `wasp start`.  ## Implementation Hints - Project path: `/home/user/taskvault` - A local PostgreSQL server is already running in this environment and is reachable at:   `postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/taskvault`   Configure the app to use it (Wasp reads the database connection string from the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable in the project\'s `.env.server` file). - To change the database backend you edit the `datasource` block\'s `provider` in `schema.prisma`; Wasp only supports `"sqlite"` or `"postgresql"`. - SQLite migrations are incompatible with PostgreSQL. Remove the existing `migrations/` directory (and clear Wasp\'s cached artifacts), then create a brand-new initial migration for PostgreSQL. After this, `migrations/migration_lock.toml` must report the `postgresql` provider. - Use Wasp\'s own database commands (`wasp db ...`) rather than calling `prisma` directly, so Wasp stays in sync. - Trigger the PgBoss job from the server setup function so it runs on every server start. - The background job must record its runs in the database. Add a new entity named `EventLog` to the data model with exactly the fields `id` (auto-increment primary key), `message` (a text/String column), and `createdAt` (a timestamp that defaults to now). This entity must be created by your new PostgreSQL migration. Each time the startup job runs it must insert exactly **one** new `EventLog` row. - The existing `GET /api/stats` endpoint must return HTTP 200 with a JSON body of the shape `{ "taskCount": <number> }`, where `<number>` is the current count of `Task` rows read from the database. - Start command: `wasp start` (the Wasp server listens on port `3001` and the web client on port `3000`). SQLite is fine for early development, but the team now needs a production-grade database and a background job queue, so the app must be migrated to **PostgreSQL**. Wasp\'s built-in background job executor, **PgBoss**, only works on PostgreSQL, so once the migration is done you must also add a PgBoss background job to justify (and exercise) the new database.  The project is a classic Wasp project: a `main.wasp` declaration file, a separate `schema.prisma` file that holds the datasource/models, a `migrations/` directory with the current SQLite migrations, and the React/Node source under `src/`. The app has a `Task` entity, a `getTasks` query, a `createTask` action, a page that lists and adds tasks, and a custom HTTP API endpoint `GET /api/stats`.  ## Requirements - Switch the app\'s database from SQLite to PostgreSQL. - Point the app at the **local** PostgreSQL server that is already running in this environment. - Regenerate the database migrations so they are PostgreSQL migrations (the old SQLite migrations cannot be reused). - Keep the existing functionality working after the migration: the task list (query + action) and the `GET /api/stats` endpoint must still work. - Add a background **job** that uses the **PgBoss** executor and runs automatically, exactly once, every time the server starts. This is only possible because the app now runs on PostgreSQL. - The app must still build and run with `wasp start`.  ## Implementation Hints - Project path: `/home/user/taskvault` - A local PostgreSQL server is already running in this environment and is reachable at:   `postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/taskvault`   Configure the app to use it (Wasp reads the database connection string from the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable in the project\'s `.env.server` file). - To change the database backend you edit the `datasource` block\'s `provider` in `schema.prisma`; Wasp only supports `"sqlite"` or `"postgresql"`. - SQLite migrations are incompatible with PostgreSQL. Remove the existing `migrations/` directory (and clear Wasp\'s cached artifacts), then create a brand-new initial migration for PostgreSQL. After this, `migrations/migration_lock.toml` must report the `postgresql` provider. - Use Wasp\'s own database commands (`wasp db ...`) rather than calling `prisma` directly, so Wasp stays in sync. - Trigger the PgBoss job from the server setup function so it runs on every server start. - The background job must record its runs in the database. Add a new entity named `EventLog` to the data model with exactly the fields `id` (auto-increment primary key), `message` (a text/String column), and `createdAt` (a timestamp that defaults to now). This entity must be created by your new PostgreSQL migration. Each time the startup job runs it must insert exactly **one** new `EventLog` row. - The existing `GET /api/stats` endpoint must return HTTP 200 with a JSON body of the shape `{ "taskCount": <number> }`, where `<number>` is the current count of `Task` rows read from the database. - Start command: `wasp start` (the Wasp server listens on port `3001` and the web client on port `3000`). SQLite is fine for early development, but the team now needs a production-grade database and a background job queue, so the app must be migrated to **PostgreSQL**. Wasp\'s built-in background job executor, **PgBoss**, only works on PostgreSQL, so once the migration is done you must also add a PgBoss background job to justify (and exercise) the new database.  The project is a classic Wasp project: a `main.wasp` declaration file, a separate `schema.prisma` file that holds the datasource/models, a `migrations/` directory with the current SQLite migrations, and the React/Node source under `src/`. The app has a `Task` entity, a `getTasks` query, a `createTask` action, a page that lists and adds tasks, and a custom HTTP API endpoint `GET /api/stats`.  ## Requirements - Switch the app\'s database from SQLite to PostgreSQL. - Point the app at the **local** PostgreSQL server that is already running in this environment. - Regenerate the database migrations so they are PostgreSQL migrations (the old SQLite migrations cannot be reused). - Keep the existing functionality working after the migration: the task list (query + action) and the `GET /api/stats` endpoint must still work. - Add a background **job** that uses the **PgBoss** executor and runs automatically, exactly once, every time the server starts. This is only possible because the app now runs on PostgreSQL. - The app must still build and run with `wasp start`.  ## Implementation Hints - Project path: `/home/user/taskvault` - A local PostgreSQL server is already running in this environment and is reachable at:   `postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/taskvault`   Configure the app to use it (Wasp reads the database connection string from the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable in the project\'s `.env.server` file). - To change the database backend you edit the `datasource` block\'s `provider` in `schema.prisma`; Wasp only supports `"sqlite"` or `"postgresql"`. - SQLite migrations are incompatible with PostgreSQL. Remove the existing `migrations/` directory (and clear Wasp\'s cached artifacts), then create a brand-new initial migration for PostgreSQL. After this, `migrations/migration_lock.toml` must report the `postgresql` provider. - Use Wasp\'s own database commands (`wasp db ...`) rather than calling `prisma` directly, so Wasp stays in sync. - Trigger the PgBoss job from the server setup function so it runs on every server start. - The background job must record its runs in the database. Add a new entity named `EventLog` to the data model with exactly the fields `id` (auto-increment primary key), `message` (a text/String column), and `createdAt` (a timestamp that defaults to now). This entity must be created by your new PostgreSQL migration. Each time the startup job runs it must insert exactly **one** new `EventLog` row. - The existing `GET /api/stats` endpoint must return HTTP 200 with a JSON body of the shape `{ "taskCount": <number> }`, where `<number>` is the current count of `Task` rows read from the database. - Start command: `wasp start` (the Wasp server listens on port `3001` and the web client on port `3000`). SQLite is fine for early development, but the team now needs a production-grade database and a background job queue, so the app must be migrated to **PostgreSQL**. Wasp\'s built-in background job executor, **PgBoss**, only works on PostgreSQL, so once the migration is done you must also add a PgBoss background job to justify (and exercise) the new database.  The project is a classic Wasp project: a `main.wasp` declaration file, a separate `schema.prisma` file that holds the datasource/models, a `migrations/` directory with the current SQLite migrations, and the React/Node source under `src/`. The app has a `Task` entity, a `getTasks` query, a `createTask` action, a page that lists and adds tasks, and a custom HTTP API endpoint `GET /api/stats`.  ## Requirements - Switch the app\'s database from SQLite to PostgreSQL. - Point the app at the **local** PostgreSQL server that is already running in this environment. - Regenerate the database migrations so they are PostgreSQL migrations (the old SQLite migrations cannot be reused). - Keep the existing functionality working after the migration: the task list (query + action) and the `GET /api/stats` endpoint must still work. - Add a background **job** that uses the **PgBoss** executor and runs automatically, exactly once, every time the server starts. This is only possible because the app now runs on PostgreSQL. - The app must still build and run with `wasp start`.  ## Implementation Hints - Project path: `/home/user/taskvault` - A local PostgreSQL server is already running in this environment and is reachable at:   `postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/taskvault`   Configure the app to use it (Wasp reads the database connection string from the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable in the project\'s `.env.server` file). - To change the database backend you edit the `datasource` block\'s `provider` in `schema.prisma`; Wasp only supports `"sqlite"` or `"postgresql"`. - SQLite migrations are incompatible with PostgreSQL. Remove the existing `migrations/` directory (and clear Wasp\'s cached artifacts), then create a brand-new initial migration for PostgreSQL. After this, `migrations/migration_lock.toml` must report the `postgresql` provider. - Use Wasp\'s own database commands (`wasp db ...`) rather than calling `prisma` directly, so Wasp stays in sync. - Trigger the PgBoss job from the server setup function so it runs on every server start. - The background job must record its runs in the database. Add a new entity named `EventLog` to the data model with exactly the fields `id` (auto-increment primary key), `message` (a text/String column), and `createdAt` (a timestamp that defaults to now). This entity must be created by your new PostgreSQL migration. Each time the startup job runs it must insert exactly **one** new `EventLog` row. - The existing `GET /api/stats` endpoint must return HTTP 200 with a JSON body of the shape `{ "taskCount": <number> }`, where `<number>` is the current count of `Task` rows read from the database. - Start command: `wasp start` (the Wasp server listens on port `3001` and the web client on port `3000`).
